question: do the street thresholds reproduce the flooding that actually happened?
answer: no, and the error is calibration rather than discrimination: at the observed peak the model marks 93% of the evaluated corridor flooded where 35% was, with recall 1.00 but a false-positive rate of 0.89

peak.source: USGS 08114000 observed gage height, cached in-repo
peak.basis: instantaneous maximum of the 15-minute series — the commensurate state for an event-maximum extent
peak.hourly_mean_note: app/public/data/replay-harvey.json peaks at this value because it is an hourly mean resample; the 0.02 ft difference is a resampling artifact, not a disagreement

observation.dataset: USGS flood-inundation extent, upper Brazos River, Aug-Sep 2017
observation.nature: water surface interpolated between 44 surveyed high-water marks and clipped to the mapped area boundary — a survey-anchored estimate, not a satellite water edge, and one maximum extent rather than a time series

method.model: flooded at the Harvey peak iff flood_stage_ft <= peak stage
method.observed: segment geometry intersects the mapped inundation extent
method.evaluated_set: segments whose centroid lies inside the mapped area boundary
method.why: outside the boundary the release supplies no observation, so scoring those segments would manufacture both error types
method.scored_at_peak: the extent is the maximum of the event, so the commensurate model state is the maximum stage; the crest moves downstream during the event, so no single gauge reading is simultaneous with every location (FINDINGS section 1)

diagnosis.note: discrimination is above chance, so the HAND height does rank ground that flooded above ground that did not; what is wrong is the absolute mapping from HAND to Richmond gauge stage

threshold_error_model.model: probit: true flood stage = shipped threshold + L + N(0, sigma); P(observed wet) = Phi((peak - L - threshold)/sigma)
threshold_error_model.reading: L is the corridor-wide average the threshold is off by; sigma is how far apart two streets with the same threshold can be. The second is much larger, and it is the one a household faces.
threshold_error_model.not_a_confusion_interval: sigma is unexplained variance from a single event, not a confidence interval on a measured quantity

estimators_of_the_same_lift.which_to_quote: the app quotes the probit fit: it uses every binary observation, and it is the fit that also yields the per-street sigma the ensemble propagates. The best-cut value maximises correct classifications on a 0.05 ft grid and is reported as the simpler corroborating estimate; the two agree to 1.4 ft
estimators_of_the_same_lift.why_they_differ: different objective functions on the same data — one counts misclassifications, the other maximises likelihood — so exact agreement would be a coincidence

correction_would_score.basis: flooded iff (threshold + lift) <= observed peak, scored on the same evaluated set as the shipped confusion matrix
correction_would_score.why_that_matters: fitted and tested on the same 1,187 outcomes, so it is an upper bound on what the correction would do rather than an out-of-sample result; spatial_holdout below is the out-of-sample test and it is weaker
correction_would_score.reading: applying the measured lift moves accuracy 0.422 -> 0.760 and the false-positive rate 0.887 -> 0.153, and recall 1.000 -> 0.597: the correction buys the ability to say DRY at the price of missing some genuinely flooded segments

below_action_stage.why_not: NO. A segment observed wet at the record peak is equally consistent with flooding at 17 ft and at 55 ft, so a point-in-time extent carries no information about a low threshold. The observation can only refute thresholds that it found DRY; it cannot confirm a low one. Adjudicating the below-action segments needs a series of extents at successive stages, which this release does not provide.
below_action_stage.note: these segments claim to submerge at or below the 20 ft action stage; the observed share is reported because it is what the test can say, not because it settles the question

false_positive_severity.note: an extent that under-represents the flood would inflate false positives; most of them sit close to the separating threshold rather than far below it

corroboration_of_closed_routes.reading: three routes that were derived from entirely different inputs (a datum comparison, a discharge conversion and an observed inundation extent) land on a constant of the same sign within a few feet of each other
corroboration_of_closed_routes.why_not_proof: the measured value is a corridor-wide optimum from ONE event, R2's is computed at the gauge reach alone, and R1's median includes its extrapolated segments -- the population is not the same, the vertical references are still not formally reconcilable, and there is no second event to test the correction on

functional_form: a constant offset generalises across halves of the corridor and a linear along-river offset does not beat it, which supports R3's conclusion in threshold_correction.py (under normal flow the physical correction is a constant offset) over the shipped summary's -0.92 ft/mile drift description
limits: one event, one extent: this measures agreement with the best available reconstruction of Harvey, and cannot be repeated on another flood from data in this repo
the extent is survey-anchored and interpolated, not observed water edges, so a segment inside it is not proven to have been flooded as a resident experienced it
the extent is the event maximum and the model state is the gauge maximum, so the downstream crest travel time (FINDINGS section 1) is not resolved here

roads are lines: any part of a segment inside the extent counts as flooded, which matches what the threshold means (a crossing point submerging) but will not match a road with one submerged low point among dry length
absolute stages still inherit the HAND-as-stage defect this test measures — that is the point, not an escape from it
consequence: no correction is applied, on the same principle as threshold_correction.py: a correction fitted to one event, with no second event to test it on, would be a new unvalidated number in place of an old one. What changes is that the error is now measured rather than declared.
